NEW YORK (CNN) -- They've been called "bromances": those buddy films and TV shows, such as the movies "Pineapple Express" and "The 40-Year-Old Virgin," that feature non-sexual but deep friendships between two or more males. Jason Segel and Paul Rudd star in "I Love You, Man," which opens Friday. The forthcoming "I Love You, Man," which opens Friday, appears to fit the bill. In the film, Paul Rudd plays a man who needs a best man for his wedding but has never made any male friends. Enter Jason Segel as Sydney Fife, whom Rudd's character, Peter Klaven, pursues on several "man-dates" that end up threatening his relationship with his fiancée (Rashida Jones). But don't call the film a "bromance" in the presence of Rudd and Segel. "We hate that word," Segel told CNN. "It was not part of the lexicon while we were filming," added Rudd. Still, both actors have plenty of experience in the, uh, guy-pal genre. Rudd has been in several comedies written, directed or produced by Judd Apatow, considered one of the leaders of the "bromance" trend with his softer, more openly emotional male characters. Segel has also been in Apatow projects -- including last year's "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" -- and he stars in the TV series "How I Met Your Mother," which finds plenty of humor in male bonding. Segel observes that what helps the films work is the discomfort of two men trying to talk about their emotions while hoping to maintain a dispassionate, hard-edged, prototypically manly façade. And he knows he's good at bringing out that discomfort in his co-stars. "Judd Apatow told me that my special skill was that I am able to maintain my likability while getting incredibly close to the creepy line, and that's what I should try to cultivate," he said. "That's what he does," Rudd noted. "He just holds [the moment] a little too long." "It's the fraction of a second too long that makes people uncomfortable," Segel added. In "I Love You, Man," Segel's character is rougher and looser than his characters in "Sarah Marshall" and "How I Met Your Mother." He welcomed the change. "It was a real treat for me, to be honest for a minute, to play this character, because I've played sort of a puppy dog guy in 'Forgetting Sarah Marshall,' and on ['Mother'] I play a husband, you know, a loving husband," he said. "So to get to play a character who is a bit more of a man of mystery was very exciting for me." In real life, claims Segel, he even has a man cave. "It's filled with puppets," he said. "And I keep wondering why I don't have a girlfriend. I'm like, 'hey, this is my house; come check it out. This is where I keep my 40 puppets.' ... I think that I have a reputation for being weird because of that." But he quickly turns serious and maintains that "I Love You, Man" does have a message to go along with its comedy. "I think we both had something to learn from each other," he said. "Paul's character had to learn that it's all right to take a little distance from your significant other and have some dude friends and someone to vent to about things you can't necessarily talk about with your girl." "Sometimes buddies hold a mirror up to the way you behave in ways that relationships with the opposite sex don't," Rudd said. "Yeah, and my character had to learn that maybe it's time to grow up a little bit," Segel added. So, this "bromance" thing, allowing a few feelings to show. Perhaps it's not so bad after all? Rudd says that the idea has its upside, despite its name. And he's glad it's been successful. "That's us in a nutshell, not macho, not tough," he said. "I think that we've all been kind of drawn to real stories, you know, characters that hopefully people can relate to and what's funny about just certain insecurites and just certain things in life. "They could easily be dramatic," he pointed out. "Just less fart jokes."

Despite their aversion to the label, both actors are well-versed in the male-bonding genre. Rudd has starred in several comedies written, directed, or produced by Judd Apatow—widely regarded as a pioneer of the trend due to his softer, more emotionally expressive male characters. Segel has similarly collaborated on Apatow projects, including last year's *Forgetting Sarah Marshall*, and currently stars in the television series *How I Met Your Mother*, which frequently mines humor from male camaraderie.

Segel observes that the success of these films hinges on the inherent awkwardness of two men attempting to express vulnerability while maintaining a stoic, prototypically masculine facade. Segel himself excels at provoking that very discomfort in his co-stars. "Judd Apatow told me that my special skill was that I am able to maintain my likability while getting incredibly close to the creepy line, and that's what I should try to cultivate," he shared. 

"That's what he does," Rudd noted. "He just holds [the moment] a little too long." 

"It's the fraction of a second too long that makes people uncomfortable," Segel added.

In *I Love You, Man*, Segel's character is rougher and more uninhibited than his previous roles in *Sarah Marshall* and *How I Met Your Mother*—a shift he eagerly welcomed. "It was a real treat for me, to be honest for a minute, to play this character, because I've played sort of a puppy dog guy in *Forgetting Sarah Marshall*, and on [*Mother*] I play a husband, you know, a loving husband," he said. "So to get to play a character who is a bit more of a man of mystery was very exciting for me."

Off-screen, Segel reveals he even maintains a personal "man cave." "It's filled with puppets," he admitted. "And I keep wondering why I don't have a girlfriend. I'm like, 'Hey, this is my house; come check it out. This is where I keep my 40 puppets.' ... I think that I have a reputation for being weird because of that."

Turning serious, Segel emphasized that *I Love You, Man* offers genuine substance alongside its comedic surface. "I think we both had something to learn from each other," he explained. "Paul's character had to learn that it's all right to take a little distance from your significant other and have some dude friends and someone to vent to about things you can't necessarily talk about with your girl."

"Sometimes buddies hold a mirror up to the way you behave in ways that relationships with the opposite sex don't," Rudd added. 

"Yeah, and my character had to learn that maybe it's time to grow up a little bit," Segel said.

Ultimately, this cinematic trend of allowing men to express emotion has real merit, despite its trendy moniker. Rudd acknowledges the concept's upside and is pleased by its resonance with audiences. "That's us in a nutshell: not macho, not tough," Rudd said. "I think that we've all been kind of drawn to real stories, you know, characters that hopefully people can relate to, and what's funny about just certain insecurities and just certain things in life."

As he pointed out, these narratives are rooted in genuine human experience: "They could easily be dramatic. Just less fart jokes."

**The Art of the Awkward Pause: How Modern Comedy Deconstructs Male Intimacy**

For decades, mainstream cinema depicted male friendship through the lens of shared activities: stoic cops chasing criminals, soldiers braving the battlefield, or slackers drinking beers while watching sports. Emotional intimacy was rarely expressed directly; instead, it was safely channeled through sarcastic jabs, shared victories, or crisis-driven solidarity. However, the rise of the modern "bromance" genre in the late 2000s fundamentally disrupted this dynamic. Films like John Hamburg’s 2009 comedy *I Love You, Man* began to explicitly examine the terror, vulnerability, and sheer discomfort men experience when navigating deep emotional bonds, creating a new comedic blueprint rooted in the tension between traditional male facades and genuine human connection.

At the center of *I Love You, Man* is Peter Klaven (Paul Rudd), an agreeable real estate agent who realizes upon getting engaged that he lacks a true best friend to serve as his Best Man. His quest to find a male confidant leads him through a series of increasingly uncomfortable "man-dates," culminating in his friendship with Sydney Fife (Jason Segel), an unapologetically open and boisterous wild card. The narrative comedy springs from the friction between Peter’s desperate desire for platonic connection and his total lack of a cultural script for how to achieve it. Traditional masculinity teaches men to project stoicism and maintain physical and emotional distance. When Peter attempts to bypass these defenses—often overcompensating with bizarre slang, forced enthusiasm, or intense eye contact—he stumbles into a minefield of social anxiety.

What elevates *I Love You, Man* from a standard buddy comedy into a masterclass in modern humor is the performance style of Rudd and Segel, particularly their mastery of comedic timing. Both actors recognize that the funniest element of male vulnerability isn't just the initial awkward statement—it is the excruciating silence that follows it. In the film, laughter is routinely generated by lingering on an uncomfortable moment just a fraction of a second longer than the audience expects. A hug that lasts two seconds too long, an overly affectionate nickname like "Jobin" that hangs unanswered in the air, or a gaze that stretches past the boundary of casual eye contact creates a palpable, hilarious tension. By refusing to let the characters quickly edit or retreat from these moments, the film forces both the protagonists and the viewer to sit in the raw, unpolished reality of attempting emotional closeness.

This micro-timing mirrors a broader cultural shift. Modern male-bonding comedies act as a safe container to explore the evolving expectations of manhood. Society increasingly encourages men to be emotionally available, sensitive, and supportive, yet the lingering ghosts of traditional masculinity tell them that showing too much affection is foolish or soft. The comedy of *I Love You, Man* thrives in this exact gray area—the collision site where old-school masculine posturing meets the modern imperative for authenticity. 

Ultimately, lingering on these awkward beats does more than just provoke laughs; it humanizes the characters. By framing the pursuit of male friendship as a high-stakes, terrifying, and clumsy endeavor, *I Love You, Man* reveals a fundamental truth about contemporary relationships: vulnerability is inherently messy. Through the expert comedic choreography of Rudd and Segel, the film demonstrates that breaking down the traditional male facade may be painfully uncomfortable, but the genuine intimacy found on the other side of that awkward pause is well worth the embarrassment.

**LOS ANGELES (CNN)** — Finding the love of your life is hard enough. But finding a guy best friend when you're already in your thirties? According to Paul Rudd and Jason Segel, that’s a whole different level of awkward.

The duo is currently taking the country by storm—and giggling their way through a coast-to-coast press tour—to promote their new comedy, *I Love You, Man*, opening in theaters nationwide this Friday. 

Directed by John Hamburg (*Along Came Polly*, co-writer of *Meet the Parents*), the film hits right at the center of a cultural moment dominated by the rise of the "bromance." But while previous comedies have flirted with male friendship as a subplot, *I Love You, Man* puts the quest for platonic male intimacy front and center.

The film stars Rudd as Peter Klaven, a straight-laced real estate agent who gets engaged to the girl of his dreams, Zooey (Rashida Jones). The problem? Peter has spent his entire adult life being a "girl’s guy" and realizes he lacks a close male friend to serve as his best man. Prompted by his fiancé and brother (Andy Samberg), Peter embarks on a series of hilarious, excruciatingly awkward "man-dates" to find a best buddy.

Enter Sydney Fife, played with casual, cargo-shorts-wearing charm by Segel. Sydney is everything Peter is not: unfiltered, emotionally available, and obsessed with playing the bass guitar.

### 'Slappin' da Bass' and Instant Chemistry

Off-screen, Rudd and Segel’s comedic chemistry is just as palpable as it is on the silver screen. During a recent interview with CNN in Los Angeles, the two actors spent half the time delivering serious answers and the other half descending into fitful bouts of laughter over inside jokes.

"We just clicked immediately," Segel said of working with Rudd. "The first day on set, we were doing a scene where we were supposed to be getting to know each other, and half of it was just us riffing and trying to make each other break. By day two, I knew this guy was going to be in my life for a long time."

Rudd agreed, noting that the premise of the movie hits on a surprisingly relatable struggle for adult men. 

"When you're a kid, you become friends with someone just because you both like the same superhero or live on the same street," Rudd told CNN. "As a grown man, how do you ask another guy for his phone number to hang out without it sounding like a pitch? It’s terrifying. You feel completely vulnerable."

That vulnerability leads to some of the movie's standout comedic moments, including Peter’s bizarre, nervous attempts at guy-slang—coining terms like "Jobin"—and an ongoing running gag involving the rock band Rush and "slappin' da bass."

### The Age of the 'Bromance'

*I Love You, Man* comes on the heels of a string of hugely successful R-rated comedies like *Knocked Up* and *Forgetting Sarah Marshall*—both of which featured Rudd and Segel in supporting or leading roles. But director John Hamburg wanted to make sure this film didn't just rely on gross-out humor, focusing instead on genuine character dynamics.

"The term 'bromance' gets thrown around a lot right now," Hamburg said at the film’s premiere. "But at its core, this is a classic romantic comedy structure—it’s just applied to two guys who really like hanging out, playing music, and eating fish tacos. Paul and Jason brought a warm, real affection to it that you can't fake."

Early tracking for the DreamWorks picture suggests strong word-of-mouth appeal, particularly among couples and groups of friends looking for a lighthearted night out. 

For Rudd and Segel, the press circuit may be wrapping up, but their newly cemented friendship appears to be the real deal. When asked if they had any advice for men out there looking to make new friends, Segel smiled, put an arm around Rudd, and offered a simple solution:

"Just go up to a guy, look him in the eye, and ask him if he wants to eat meatball subs and play bass. If he says no, he was never worth it anyway."

*I Love You, Man* opens in theaters Friday. It is rated R for pervasive language and crude sexual humor.

**CNN.com** — Entertainment

# 'Slap da bass': Paul Rudd and Jason Segel on the art of the 'bromance'

**By David Chi**  
**CNN Entertainment**

**(CNN)** — In a dimly lit suite at the Beverly Hilton, Paul Rudd and Jason Segel are engaged in a passionate, highly technical debate about the comedic merits of the phrase "jobin." 

"It’s just a great word," Segel says, leaning back on a plush couch with a lazy, infectious grin. "It sounds like a guy who wears cargo shorts and drinks IPA at 11:00 a.m."

"It has a real bounce to it," Rudd agrees, deadpanning effortlessly. "It’s high-level vocabulary."

If the dynamic feels completely unscripted, that’s because the chemistry between the two actors is very real. It’s also the engine driving their new comedy, *I Love You, Man*, opening in theaters nationwide this Friday. 

Directed by John Hamburg (*Along Came Polly*), the film follows Peter Klaven (Rudd), a straight-laced real estate agent engaged to the woman of his dreams (Rashida Jones). There’s just one problem: Peter has no male friends, meaning no best man for the wedding. Enter Sydney Fife (Segel), a charismatic, man-cave-dwelling musician who eats fish tacos, plays bass, and doesn't care about societal conventions.

What follows is a hilarious, cringeworthy, and surprisingly sweet courtship—only this time, it’s between two straight guys.

### The Era of the 'Bromance'

In 2009, pop culture has found a sticky new buzzword for this dynamic: the "bromance." While the term has been floating around frat houses and pop-psychology blogs for a few years, *I Love You, Man* threatens to put it squarely in the mainstream lexicon. 

Both actors, however, regard the trendy label with a mix of affection and mild skepticism. 

"It’s funny that we needed to invent a whole new word just to describe two guys being nice to each other," Rudd says with a chuckle. "Women can have deep, emotional friendships and nobody bats an eye. But if two dudes want to hang out, eat lunch, and jam out to Rush, suddenly we need a brand-new linguistic category."

"Guys are traditionally terrible at making friends once they hit adulthood," Segel adds. "When you're a kid, you just walk up to someone on the playground and say, 'Hey, you like Batman? I like Batman. We’re best friends.' But when you’re 30? It’s terrifying. It feels like dating. You’re sitting by the phone wondering, 'Is it too soon to text him? Did I say something weird when I said goodbye?' That awkwardness is really what the movie is about."

### The Apatow Effect

While *I Love You, Man* is directed by Hamburg, the shadow of comedy titan Judd Apatow looms large over the project. Rudd and Segel are key members of what Hollywood has dubbed the "Apatow Mafia"—a loose collective of actors, writers, and directors who have revolutionized film comedy over the last five years. 

From *The 40-Year-Old Virgin* and *Knocked Up* to last year’s hit *Forgetting Sarah Marshall* (written by and starring Segel, with Rudd turning in a memorable cameo as a dim-witted surf instructor), the Apatow school of filmmaking has swapped out the glossy, high-concept gags of the 1990s for something far more vulnerable, improvised, and male-centric.

"Judd really opened the door for comedies that allow men to be sensitive idiots," Segel says. "Before that wave, male leads in comedies were usually either cool schemers or cartoon characters. Judd showed that you could center a film on guys who are genuinely insecure, who talk about their feelings, but are still hilariously flawed."

Rudd nods in agreement. "There’s a real honesty to it. Working in that circle taught us to trust our instincts and improvise. On set with Jason, half the fun was just pushing the scene until one of us cracked up. When you have that foundation of trust, the audience feels it. You’re not just watching actors read lines; you’re watching a real dynamic unfold."

### Puppets, Bass, and Male Bonding

That shared sensibility extends to their off-screen lives, though their personal hobbies couldn't be more different. While Rudd is famously low-key, Segel has developed a reputation in Hollywood for a rather unusual passion: puppet theater. 

Fans of *Forgetting Sarah Marshall* will recall Segel's character writing a Dracula-themed puppet musical—a subplot taken directly from Segel’s real life. 

"I am completely serious about puppets," Segel insists, when asked if the hobby was just a bit for the movies. "I have a house full of them. People think it's a bit creepy, but I genuinely think Jim Henson was a genius. I’m actually working on a pitch right now to bring the Muppets back to the big screen."

Rudd breaks into a grin, shaking his head. "I remember the first time I went over to Jason’s place. You expect a bachelor pad with a big TV. Instead, you walk in and there’s a felt vampire staring at you from the corner. It’s alarming, but you gotta respect the commitment."

"Hey, Sydney Fife has his man-cave, I have my puppets," Segel laughs. "Every guy needs a weird sanctuary."

As the press tour winds down and the film hits multiplexes, both stars hope *I Love You, Man* does more than just make audiences laugh—they hope it encourages guys everywhere to open up a little, even if it’s awkward.

"If a guy walks out of this theater and feels inspired to call up his buddy and say, 'Hey man, I love you,' then we’ve done our jobs," Rudd says. 

"Or at least," Segel interjects, "call him up and ask him to slap da bass."

**HOLLYWOOD — March 2009**

Inside a dimly lit room at the Four Seasons Hotel, Paul Rudd and Jason Segel are losing their minds. 

They are supposed to be answering a standard junket question about their new comedy, *I Love You, Man*. Instead, Rudd is doing an impression of a bizarre, high-pitched reggae artist, and Segel is doubled over, tears streaming down his face, clutching his stomach in hyperventilating laughter. 

"I don't even know what we're talking about anymore," Segel wheezes, wiping his eyes. 

"We’re talking about love, man," Rudd replies smoothly, breaking into a sly, dimpled grin. "Pure, unadulterated male love."

The clip, which has already begun tearing through the early iterations of viral internet video, is more than just a hilarious junket derailment. It is the thesis statement for a full-blown Hollywood phenomenon. 

In the late 2000s, Tinseltown found its most lucrative and culturally defining subgenre not in superhero origin stories or high-concept sci-fi, but in the tender, awkward, and deeply affectionate space between two guys. 

They call it the "bromance"—and *I Love You, Man* is its crowning achievement.

---

### The Evolution of the "Man-Date"

For decades, male relationships in American cinema were defined by bullets or banter. You had the stoic action partners (*Lethal Weapon*), the mismatched odd couples (*Planes, Trains and Automobiles*), or the crude party animals (*Animal House*). Emotional vulnerability was rarely on the table, unless someone was bleeding out in a trench.

Then came the Judd Apatow revolution of the mid-2000s. Movies like *Anchorman*, *40-Year-Old Virgin*, *Knocked Up*, and *Superbad* introduced a new archetype of American man: sensitive, slightly emotionally stunted, intensely loyal, and entirely unafraid to tell his best friend he loved him—even if it was cloaked in a layer of stoner absurdity.

By 2009, the concept had evolved from a subplot to the main event. 

Directed by John Hamburg, *I Love You, Man* stars Rudd as Peter Klaven, a real estate agent engaged to the woman of his dreams (Rashida Jones) who suddenly realizes he has no male friends to be his best man. Enter Sydney Fife (Segel), a charismatic, free-spirited bass player who lives in a converted Venice Beach garage. 

Unlike traditional romantic comedies, the emotional stakes of the film don't hinge on whether Peter gets the girl—he already has her. The film hinges on whether Peter and Sydney can overcome their insecurities, learn to "slap da bass," and commit to a lifelong platonic connection.

"It’s a romantic comedy where the couple happens to be two dudes," Segel explained during a calmer moment of the press tour. "Guys in our generation are dynamic. We want to talk about sports, yeah, but we also get lonely. We want a buddy to hang out with, drink a beer, and talk about our feelings without it being weird."

---

### Chemistry You Can’t Script

What makes *I Love You, Man* stand out in the late-2000s comedy wave is the unforced, almost chaotic chemistry between its leads. 

Rudd, the king of deadpan absurdity, and Segel, the master of puppy-dog earnestness, had already shared screen time in 2008’s *Forgetting Sarah Marshall*. But paired together as co-leads, their off-screen friendship bled into every frame of the film—and every interview on the press circuit.

During their junket circuit, journalists quickly gave up on asking traditional questions. Interviewing Rudd and Segel felt less like a media junket and more like eavesdropping on two college roommates who had consumed too much iced coffee. They made up fictional backstory characters ("Gideon"), riffed on nonsensical phrases like "Jobin," and relentlessly flirted with each other in front of the cameras.

"You can't fake the kind of comfort where you’re willing to look completely stupid in front of another guy," Rudd noted. "That’s what male friendship actually is. It’s 90 percent inside jokes that nobody else finds funny, and 10 percent holding each other up when life gets weird."

This off-screen dynamic tapped into a broader cultural shift. In the late 2000s, terms like "man-date" and "bromance" officially entered the Merriam-Webster lexicon. Sociologists began writing papers on the declining stigma around male intimacy. The late-2000s comedy didn't invent the concept of male friendship, but it gave young men permission to embrace it publicly.

---

### The Legacy of the "Slap-Da-Bass" Era

As the decade draws to a close, *I Love You, Man* feels like the apex of a specific cinematic golden era. It sits comfortably alongside *Step Brothers*, *Pineapple Express*, and *The Hangover*—films that recognized that the funniest, sweetest, and most chaotic relationships in adult life are often the ones we build with our friends.

Back at the Four Seasons, the interview is wrapping up. Segel and Rudd are being signaled by a publicist that their time is over. 

Segel looks over at Rudd, affectionately punching his shoulder. "I love you, man," he says, mimicking the line from the movie, but with a crack of genuine warmth.

Rudd smiles, leaning into his trademark awkwardness, and whispers back in his best slacker voice: "I love you, broseph."

The room erupts into laughter one last time. Hollywood may move on to new trends, but for a few years in the late 2000s, the greatest love stories in movies were the ones between the boys.

**Paul Rudd, Jason Segel talk 'I Love You, Man' — and why they cringe at the word 'bromance'**

**LOS ANGELES (CNN)** — Paul Rudd and Jason Segel are sitting in a Beverly Hills hotel suite, visibly exhausted by the press junket machine, yet effortlessly cracking each other up. They are ostensibly here to promote their new comedy, *I Love You, Man*, but they have one small request for the media: Please, stop using the word "bromance."

"It’s just a terrible word, isn’t it?" Rudd says, leaning forward and lowering his voice as if sharing a secret. "It sounds like a brand of cheap body spray you’d buy at a gas station. 'New from Axe: *Bromance*.'"

Segel nods vigorously in agreement. "It cheapens the whole thing! It’s like language gave up. Why do we need a special portmanteau just to describe two guys who happen to be friends? Can’t it just be a 'friendship'?"

"Or a romance," Rudd interrupts with a deadpan expression. "Keep it simple. Either we're friends, or we're deeply, passionately in love. Don't invent a middle ground."

### Searching for a Best Man

In *I Love You, Man*, directed by John Hamburg (*Along Came Polly*), Rudd plays Peter Klaven, a straight-laced real estate agent who gets engaged to the woman of his dreams (Rashida Jones). There’s just one problem: Peter has spent his entire adult life focusing on girlfriends and has no close male friends. Faced with the daunting task of finding a Best Man for his upcoming wedding, Peter embarks on a series of awkward "man-dates."

Enter Sydney Fife, played by Segel. Sydney is everything Peter is not: messy, wildly confident, emotionally open, and obsessed with Rush. The two strike up an instant, genuine connection over jam sessions in Sydney’s "man cave" and shared slushes at the boardwalk.

While the premise inevitably sparked the Hollywood buzzword *du jour*, both actors insist the movie is tapping into something far more relatable—and awkward—than a simple pop-culture catchphrase.

"Making friends as an adult guy is genuinely terrifying," Segel says. "When you're a kid, you just walk up to someone on the playground and say, 'Hey, do you like Transformers?' and boom, you're best friends. When you're 30, approaching another guy to hang out feels like asking him on a date. You're terrified of rejection."

Rudd agrees. "The movie hits on a real vulnerability. Guys aren't socialized to seek out male companionship in a romantic-comedy kind of way. Peter is totally lost. He doesn't know the rules. He tries to sound cool, he invents weird slang, he calls Sydney 'Jobin' for no reason. It's painful because it's true."

### On-Screen Chemistry, Off-Screen Chaos

The dynamic between Rudd and Segel feels less like a rehearsed movie pairing and more like two old college roommates who share endless inside jokes. The duo previously shared the screen in 2008's smash hit *Forgetting Sarah Marshall*, but *I Love You, Man* places their banter front and center.

Much of the film’s dialogue was forged through improvisation on set, particularly during the scenes where Sydney teaches Peter how to "slap da bass"—a ridiculous homage to 1970s progressive rock that has already become the film's breakout running gag.

"Paul is a nightmare to work with because he refuses to break character, but he makes *you* break," Segel jokes. "He will look you dead in the eye and say the absolute dumbest thing imaginable with total conviction, and you're just sitting there ruining a take because you're crying laughing."

"I take my bass-slapping very seriously, Jason," Rudd replies smoothly. "It’s an art form."

### Moving Past the Buzzwords

As the film prepares to hit theaters nationwide this Friday, both stars hope audiences look past the marketing labels and connect with the heart of the story. 

"At the end of the day, it's a movie about loneliness and finding your person—whether that's your wife or your best friend," Segel says. "It just happens to have a lot of fart jokes and bass guitar solos."

And as for the 'B-word'? 

"We're launching a personal campaign to ban it," Rudd smiles. "If anyone asks me about our 'bromance' on the red carpet tonight, I'm just going to stare at them silently until they feel as awkward as my character in the movie."

*I Love You, Man* opens in theaters nationwide this Friday.

**NEW YORK (CNN) --** In a Hollywood landscape long dominated by high-octane action films and traditional boy-meets-girl romantic comedies, a different kind of love story has taken center stage: the "bromance." With the release of *I Love You, Man*, stars Paul Rudd and Jason Segel are diving headfirst into the awkward, untamed territory of adult male friendship—and they aren't afraid to get vulnerable.

Directed by John Hamburg, the film follows Peter Klaven (Rudd), a successful, straight-laced real estate agent who makes a sudden realization upon getting engaged: he has no male friends, and consequently, no one to serve as his best man. What follows is a series of cringe-inducing "man-dates" as Peter attempts to forge a meaningful platonic connection, eventually landing on Sydney Fife (Segel), a charismatic, fiercely independent bachelor.

While the premise serves up plenty of laugh-out-loud moments, the film hits a deeper nerve by examining the dynamics of modern male relationships. Unlike classic buddy comedies that rely heavily on macho bravado or reluctant partnerships, *I Love You, Man* focuses on the genuine difficulty adult men face when trying to make friends—and the emotional openness required to sustain those bonds.

"Men are traditionally terrible at being vulnerable with one another," Rudd noted during press rounds in New York. "We tend to hide behind sports, work, or busting each other's chops. This movie leans into the discomfort of a guy actually admitting he's lonely and putting himself out there. It’s essentially a romantic comedy, just between two dudes."

Segel’s character acts as the uninhibited catalyst to Rudd’s neurotic, guarded protagonist. Sydney encourages Peter to shed his social anxieties, let down his guard, and embrace his authentic self—whether that means jamming out to the rock band Rush or literally screaming at the top of his lungs on a boardwalk.

"Sydney doesn't care about societal expectations of masculinity; he cares about being real," Segel said of his character. "There’s a freedom in vulnerability that a lot of guys are taught to resist. Showing that two men can support each other emotionally without it being a punchline was really important to us."

The effortless, improvisational chemistry between the two leads comes as no surprise to comedy fans. Both Rudd and Segel are key figures in the informal troupe of actors assembled by producer-director Judd Apatow. Having previously shared the screen in Apatow-produced hits like *Knocked Up* and *Forgetting Sarah Marshall*, the duo brings a familiar brand of tender-hearted, R-rated humor to this project.

While Apatow himself was not involved in *I Love You, Man*, his influence is palpable. The "Apatow era" redefined modern cinematic masculinity, swapping out invulnerable alpha males for flawed, sensitive men navigating adulthood. Rudd and Segel carry that torch forward, pushing the subgenre into new territory where expressing genuine affection for a friend—saying the titular "I love you, man"—is the ultimate triumph.

Ultimately, *I Love You, Man* offers more than just memorable catchphrases and bass-guitar riffs. It serves as a comedic reflection of a culture where men are increasingly allowed—and expected—to share their feelings. By treating the search for a best friend with the same gravity and sweet sentiment usually reserved for romance, Rudd and Segel prove that opening up might just be the ultimate test of manhood.
